newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Italy, France seek end to EMU delay talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy, France seek end to EMU delay talk.

text.p: Is Europe's single currency heading for trouble or delay? The answer on Thursday once again depended on who was being asked.
France's president and Italy's prime minister sought to staunch any talk of a delay to economic and monetary union -- a move that many politicians fear would kill the project off.

The Bundesbank president, however, remained decidedly gloomy about the prospect of life under a single currency -- unless European Union governments truly got their finances in shape and kept them there.

Forecasters said Germany's economy, for one, was not playing along. In fact, the already worrying jobless rate was likely to grow, adding strains to Germany's ability to make the single currency grade.
U.S. investment house Goldman Sachs reckoned the politicians would win out. It predicted the euro would start on time in January, 1999.
Talk of delay to the single currency, which has become rife in unofficial circles for much of February, pushed France's Jacques Chirac and Italy's Romano Prodi to action.
French officials announced that the two had spoken on the telephone and that: "Each man reaffirmed his determination to see his country join the euro at the planned date."
Sources said that Chirac had made the call in part to assure the Italian that Paris and Bonn were not planning a delay behind Rome's back.
One element behind the talk of a delay has been that Germany and France need to find a way to keep Italy's weaker economy out of the first wave of countries to adopt the currency.
Later, Prodi made his own view clear -- that Italy did not want to be let in unless it truly qualified.
"Italy will not ask for a delay or easy terms. Italy is in a condition to undergo the test that all European countries have to undergo for the single currency," he told the Senate in Rome.
One of Prodi's political allies, however, was not so sure. The leader of Italy's far-left Communist Refoundation party, Fausto Bertinotti, said Rome should seek a deal to delay EMU.
Away from the politics, however, German money men continued to worry about coal-face economics.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer warned against an unstable euro and unsustainable budgetary rigour.

He said EU countries' failure to maintain budgetary discipline could lead to wage conflicts, higher unemployment, a greater burden on welfare systems and political pressure on the future European Central Bank to loosen monetary policy.
Germany's Ifo economic institute was similarly gloomy -- but about the immediate state of the economy.
It said it expected jobless levels to reach 10.9 percent in 1997, up from 10.4 percent last year.
Another element in the delay talk has been than Germany's dole queues will stifle Bonn's ability to cut the country's deficit to qualify for EMU.
The economists at Goldman Sachs said that although slow economic growth could still derail EMU, the betting was still that the deadline would be met.
"We do think that the most likely event is that a start date of 1999 does get met," Gavyn Davies, chief international economist for Goldman Sachs International told a conference in Frankfurt.
His colleague, Thomas Mayer, added that Germany would "find a way" to consolidate its public finances sufficiently to qualify.
